reviews.summary: The manuscript is technically credible and the privacy/engineering claims hold up, but several clinical-content claims do not match Turkish primary-care reality or the source code itself. Most importantly: (1) the manuscript states HbA1c is one of the principal continuous analytes generated for the DM module and shown in Figure 1, but inspection of src/syntha/fhir/codes.py shows HbA1c is NOT in LAB_LOINC — only a SNOMED 'HbA1c measurement' procedure is emitted in diabetes.py, with no Observation carrying LOINC 4548-4. This contradicts the abstract/methods/results and is misleading. (2) The default first-line antihypertensive is lisinopril (RxNorm 314076) — in Turkey, perindopril and ramipril dominate ACEi prescribing, lisinopril is uncommon; for ARB the choice of losartan is fine but valsartan/telmisartan are more typical. (3) The IHD module per Table 1 says 'Aspirin + statin + beta-blocker' but Turkish/ESC post-MI/CCS practice would also expect a high-intensity statin and an ACEi/ARB if EF reduced; the beta-blocker default is metoprolol succinate while nebivolol/bisoprolol/carvedilol dominate Turkish cardiology. (4) Multiple ICD-10 codes are at .9 unspecified granularity (I25.9, J45.9, J44.9, E78.5, F32.9, F41.9, N18.9, E07.9) — the manuscript acknowledges this in Limitations item (vi) but the wording 'flagged for clinician curation' undersells that the source signal (e.g., asthma severity, CKD stage from eGFR which IS present, F32 severity from PHQ-9 which IS calculated) could drive far more specific codes; this is a downstream patient-safety concern for any model trained on these data. (5) The 'pristine-healthy cohort' framing is honest in Limitations but the Discussion's claim that syntha is useful for 'training risk-prediction models' should be more sharply caveated — by construction the comorbidity prevalences (HT 7.5%, DM 4.8%) are far below TÜİK figures (TURDEP-II DM ~13.7%, PatenT-2 HT ~30%), so any risk model trained on syntha will be miscalibrated for the general Turkish population. (6) DM_Komplikasyonlu maps to E11.8 + SNOMED 44054006 — defensible per the in-code comment, but the manuscript should explicitly state this T2DM assumption rather than presenting 'Diabetes' generically. (7) Buspirone as the default anxiolytic is unusual in Turkish primary care (SSRIs dominate, then benzodiazepines short-term); flagging buspirone as 'first-line anxiety' in the code is at odds with both Turkish and most international guidelines. (8) Tiotropium is in the LABA list — tiotropium is a LAMA, not a LABA; this is a coding-correctness bug that propagates to FHIR output. (9) Reference ranges are mostly defensible and sex-aware for Hb/creatinine, but ALT M ≤ 50 / F ≤ 38 in the notes column is at odds with the COMMON entry (7–56 sex-agnostic) — sex-specific ALT cut-offs should be enforced as in BY_SEX. No critical patient-harm issues if the tool is used as intended (synthetic-only research), but the HbA1c discrepancy, the tiotropium=LABA bug, and the Turkish drug-default mismatches together warrant major revision before publication.

critical_issues.section: Methods – Synthea-style clinical modules + Results Figure 1
critical_issues.quote: Per-lab time series are reconstructed by an AR(1) walk backward from the cross-sectional `_latest` value, using column-specific Westgard analytical CVs (eGFR 6% + 1%/yr secular decline, HbA1c σ ≈ 0.3%, Hb 2%, ALT/AST 15%, TG 15%).' and 'Figure 1 ... overlays empirical density estimates for the principal continuous analytes (systolic BP, diastolic BP, HbA1c, fasting glucose, ...)
critical_issues.issue: The manuscript repeatedly treats HbA1c as a modeled continuous lab with AR(1) drift and a panel-validated marginal, but src/syntha/fhir/codes.py LAB_LOINC has NO HbA1c entry (no LOINC 4548-4 or 17856-6). diabetes.py emits only a SNOMED procedure code (313835008) for 'HbA1c measurement' — no Observation resource with a numeric value. This makes the DM module clinically incomplete: a diabetes Encounter with no HbA1c Observation is not how Turkish ambulatory diabetes care looks. Either HbA1c is actually emitted (and the LOINC table is wrong) or it isn't (and the abstract/methods/results are wrong).
critical_issues.fix: Add LOINC 4548-4 (HbA1c % NGSP) or 17856-6 (HbA1c IFCC mmol/mol) to LAB_LOINC with UCUM '%' or 'mmol/mol', wire it into the copula marginals, emit an Observation in diabetes.py with the procedure result, and reconcile the Methods/Figure 1 text. If HbA1c is genuinely not generated, remove all claims that it is, including the AR(1) σ ≈ 0.3% line, and add to Limitations that the DM module currently emits no quantitative HbA1c.

critical_issues.quote: BRONCHODILATORS_LABA = [("637202", "Tiotropium Bromide 0.018 MG Inhalation Capsule", "1 capsule daily")]' and Table 1 'COPD | KOAH | LAMA + LABA
critical_issues.issue: Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA), NOT a LABA. Table 1 promises 'LAMA + LABA' but the code emits LAMA + LAMA. There is no actual LABA (formoterol/salmeterol/olodaterol/indacaterol) in the prescription set. A FHIR Bundle for a KOAH patient will therefore mis-represent GOLD-recommended therapy, and any downstream Turkish pharmacy/SGK ETL will flag this.
critical_issues.fix: Either rename the constant BRONCHODILATORS_LAMA and add a true BRONCHODILATORS_LABA list (e.g., RxNorm for salmeterol or formoterol; or use a fixed LAMA/LABA combination SCD such as umeclidinium/vilanterol), and update Table 1 to honestly state what is emitted. In Turkey, tiotropium (Spiriva) + formoterol/budesonide or fluticasone/vilanterol combinations are most common — pick a defensible pair.

major_issues.section: Methods – Synthea-style clinical modules / Table 1 / rxnorm.py
major_issues.quote: Hypertension | HT | ACEi or ARB | Stage-2 → dual therapy
major_issues.issue: The hard-coded ACEi default is lisinopril 10 mg (RxNorm 314076). Lisinopril is a US-formulary default; in Turkish primary care the dominant ACEi by SGK prescription volume are perindopril (Coversyl) and ramipril (Delix), with lisinopril rarely chosen. The ARB default is losartan, which is reasonable, but valsartan and telmisartan are more frequently prescribed. The dual-therapy logic also picks losartan as the second agent after lisinopril — ACEi + ARB combination is contraindicated (ONTARGET, KDIGO). Stage-2 patients in Turkish/ESC practice get ACEi-or-ARB + CCB (amlodipine) or + thiazide-like diuretic, never ACEi + ARB.
major_issues.fix: Replace lisinopril with perindopril 5 mg (RxNorm e.g. 854255) or ramipril 5 mg (RxNorm 261962) as the Turkish-defensible default; ensure the second agent for stage-2 is amlodipine or HCTZ, NOT losartan after lisinopril. Document the change as a Turkish-locale default in the methods and update Table 1 accordingly. Cite the Türk Hipertansiyon Uzlaşı Raporu / TKD HT guideline.

major_issues.section: Methods – Synthea-style clinical modules / rxnorm.py BETA_BLOCKERS / IHD module
major_issues.quote: Ischemic heart disease | IKH | Aspirin + statin + beta-blocker | —' with BETA_BLOCKERS default metoprolol succinate 50 mg
major_issues.issue: For IHD/post-MI in Turkish cardiology practice, nebivolol, bisoprolol, and carvedilol dominate; metoprolol succinate (Beloc-ZOK) is also used but is one of many. More importantly, the IHD module is missing an ACEi/ARB, which is a Class I recommendation in ESC 2023 Chronic Coronary Syndromes guidelines (which TKD follows) for post-MI/CCS patients with HF, HTN, DM or LV dysfunction. Stage-aware logic should also distinguish CCS vs ACS context.
major_issues.fix: Add an ACEi/ARB to the IKH module (perindopril or ramipril) and update Table 1 to 'Aspirin + high-intensity statin + beta-blocker + ACEi/ARB'. Consider adding nebivolol as an alternative beta-blocker reflecting Turkish prescribing patterns. Reference ESC 2023 CCS / TKD post-MI guidance.

major_issues.section: Methods – Synthea-style clinical modules / rxnorm.py ANXIOLYTICS
major_issues.quote: Anxiety | Anksiyete | SSRI | GAD-7 ≥ 10' with ANXIOLYTICS = [Buspirone 10 MG]
major_issues.issue: Table 1 says anxiety first-line = SSRI, but the rxnorm ANXIOLYTICS constant points to buspirone, which is essentially absent from Turkish primary-care prescribing (not even consistently on SGK formulary as first-line). NICE, APA, and Türkiye Psikiyatri Derneği consensus all place SSRI/SNRI as first-line for GAD; buspirone is an adjunct/alternative at best. If buspirone is actually emitted alongside or instead of an SSRI, this misrepresents Turkish anxiety care.
major_issues.fix: Either (a) remove buspirone and have the anxiety module reuse SSRIS (escitalopram is the most common Turkish first-line for GAD), or (b) keep buspirone explicitly as a tertiary alternative and document that. Update Table 1 if behavior differs from 'SSRI'.

major_issues.section: Methods – FHIR R4 export / fhir/codes.py CONDITION_ICD10
major_issues.quote: ICD-10 specificity is currently at unspecified `.9` granularity for several conditions, flagged for clinician curation.
major_issues.issue: The .9 fall-back undersells available source signal: (a) Asthma J45.9 — source could yield J45.20/J45.30/J45.40/J45.50 if severity/control is inferable; (b) COPD J44.9 — could be J44.0 (with acute lower respiratory infection) or J44.1 (with acute exacerbation) given the encounter context; (c) CKD N18.9 — eGFR IS modeled, so N18.1–N18.5 stage codes are derivable and would be far more useful for downstream ML; (d) Depression F32.9 — PHQ-9 ≥ 10 is computed, so F32.0/F32.1/F32.2 (mild/moderate/severe) are derivable; (e) E78.5 hyperlipidaemia — LDL/TG are modeled, so E78.0 (pure hypercholesterolaemia), E78.1 (pure hyperglyceridaemia), E78.2 (mixed) are derivable. Leaving everything at .9 makes the dataset markedly less useful for clinical-coding research, undersells the source signal, and risks downstream models learning to predict unspecified codes — a real patient-safety implication when used for autocoder training.
major_issues.fix: Implement a small ICD-10 specificity layer that uses the already-modeled lab/score columns to refine: eGFR→N18.x stage; PHQ-9→F32.x severity; LDL/TG profile→E78.x; encounter reason text or comorbidity combo→J44.0/J44.1; spirometry-free fallback to J45.909 'Unspecified asthma, uncomplicated' is also more honest than J45.9. Expand Limitations item (vi) to acknowledge the autocoder-training risk.

major_issues.quote: Synthetic disease prevalence is below TÜİK national figures by construction of the pristine-healthy source (HT ≈ 7.5%, DM ≈ 4.8%, hyperlipidemia ≈ 12%, thyroid ≈ 14.5%, depression ≈ 0.22%, anxiety ≈ 1.1%, cancer ≈ 1.4%); calibration is queued for v0.6.
major_issues.issue: The framing is honest but understates the implications. TURDEP-II reports adult DM prevalence ~13.7%, PatenT-2 reports HT ~30%, TEKHARF reports hyperlipidaemia >40% above age 40; syntha's 4.8% DM and 7.5% HT are 3–4× lower. A depression prevalence of 0.22% versus Turkish primary-care depression rates of 10–20% is two orders of magnitude off. Calling this a 'pristine-healthy' cohort and then proposing it for 'training risk-prediction models' (Discussion paragraph 1) is internally inconsistent — any prevalence-sensitive model trained on syntha will be miscalibrated and may underestimate risk in deployment, a patient-safety concern if such a model is then deployed without recalibration.
major_issues.fix: Move the prevalence-mismatch caveat from Limitations into the Discussion's use-case paragraph, explicitly state that risk-prediction models trained on syntha must be recalibrated against TÜİK / TURDEP-II / PatenT-2 / TEKHARF marginals before any prospective use, and remove or qualify 'training risk-prediction models' as a primary use case. Reference TURDEP-II (Satman 2013) and PatenT-2.

major_issues.quote: Reference-range coverage for the 14 sex-aware analytes is reported per cohort in `validation_report.json`
major_issues.issue: The text claims 14 'sex-aware' analytes, but BY_SEX in reference_ranges.py contains only hemoglobin and creatinine — 2 columns, not 14. Other columns where sex differences are clinically meaningful (HDL ≥40 M / ≥50 F, ALT ≤50 M / ≤38 F as the in-code notes themselves acknowledge, ferritin M 30–400 / F 13–150 also acknowledged in notes) are encoded sex-agnostically in COMMON despite the notes flagging the discrepancy. Calling 14 analytes 'sex-aware' is incorrect.
major_issues.fix: Either move HDL, ALT, AST (mildly), ferritin into BY_SEX with sex-specific bounds and then truthfully claim sex-awareness, or change the manuscript text to '2 sex-aware analytes (hemoglobin, creatinine); 12 sex-agnostic analytes with sex-specific notes pending v0.6.' Cite Turkish reference-interval studies (e.g., Türk Klinik Biyokimya Derneği) if you tighten the ranges.

major_issues.quote: RiskAssessment (Charlson Comorbidity Index, LOINC 75618-7; calibrated 10-year mortality $P = 1 - 0.983^{0.9\cdot\text{CCI}}$)
major_issues.issue: (a) LOINC 75618-7 is 'Charlson comorbidity index [Score]' — correct as a LOINC for the score itself, but the RiskAssessment.prediction.outcome should additionally carry SNOMED 419099009 (Dead) and use Quantity for probabilityDecimal — please confirm. (b) The formula 1 − 0.983^(0.9·CCI) is the age-adjusted CCI mortality function from Charlson 1994 (the original 1987 paper used 0.983^CCI without the 0.9 age weight), so cite Charlson 1994 (Charlson ME et al., J Clin Epidemiol 1994;47:1245-51) not the 1987 Charlson reference [20]. (c) For a pristine-healthy cohort the CCI will be near-zero by construction, so the predicted 10-yr mortality is uniformly ~1.7% — clinically meaningless for risk stratification. Either flag this in Limitations or do not emit RiskAssessment for CCI=0.
major_issues.fix: Update reference [20] to Charlson 1994 (or add it as a separate reference for the age-adjusted formula). Add a note that RiskAssessment for the pristine cohort is dominated by floor effects. Verify RiskAssessment.prediction.outcome carries an appropriate SNOMED 'death' code.

major_issues.section: Methods – FHIR R4 export / PHQ-9 GAD-7 / fhir/codes.py CONDITION_SNOMED
major_issues.quote: PHQ-9 (LOINC 44261-6) and GAD-7 (LOINC 70274-6) observations are conditionally emitted.' and CONDITION_SNOMED 'Anksiyete: 48694002 Anxiety (finding)
major_issues.issue: (a) SNOMED 48694002 is 'Anxiety' as a finding, not the disorder. For an Anksiyete diagnosis the FHIR-preferred code is 197480006 (Anxiety disorder) or 48694002 should at least be paired with a finding-vs-disorder note. (b) PHQ-9 LOINC 44261-6 is the panel total score; the 9 individual item LOINCs (44250-9 through 44258-2 + 44259-0) are commonly expected by HAPI servers as components. Confirm whether syntha emits items or only the total.
major_issues.fix: Switch Anksiyete SNOMED to 197480006 (Anxiety disorder). Document whether PHQ-9/GAD-7 are emitted as panel-total only or with per-item components; if total-only, note in Methods that downstream consumers expecting item-level coding will need to flatten.

major_issues.quote: syntha is trained on two nested anonymized retrospective Turkish cohorts curated upstream by the data steward at Acibadem University: a "tolerant" cohort (n=135,569 episodes) and a strict subset (n=55,141) retained only when all clinical-pristine quality filters pass.
major_issues.issue: The cohort is described as 'pristine-healthy', but the comorbidity prevalence table in Limitations shows HT 7.5%, DM 4.8%, hyperlipidaemia 12%, thyroid 14.5%, cancer 1.4% — these are non-trivial prevalences for a 'pristine' cohort, suggesting the curation filters do not actually exclude disease but rather exclude noisy/dirty records. The semantic mismatch between 'pristine-healthy' and the actual disease prevalence undermines the framing. Also, the IRB / ethics approval number for the upstream de-identification is not stated.
major_issues.fix: Either rename to 'data-quality-curated' or 'noise-filtered' cohort and reserve 'pristine-healthy' for a true zero-comorbidity slice. State the Acibadem IRB / ethics committee approval number and date for the upstream de-identification, even though this work involves no patient interaction — Turkish KVKK and Helsinki disclosure norms expect it.

minor_issues.quote: "Kanser": "Habis neoplazi"
minor_issues.issue: 'Habis neoplazi' is technically correct medical Turkish but is unusual in clinical Turkish charting; clinicians more commonly write 'Malign neoplazi' or simply 'Kanser'/'Malignite'. 'Habis' (= malignant, lit. 'malicious') is older Ottoman-influenced terminology.
minor_issues.fix: Change to 'Malign neoplazi' or 'Malignite' for modern clinical-Turkish naturalness. Keep 'Habis neoplazi' only as a synonym.

minor_issues.quote: "Anksiyete": "Anksiyete bozukluğu"
minor_issues.issue: Otherwise the displays mostly use the bare term (Depresyon, Hipertansiyon, Hiperlipidemi) — adding 'bozukluğu' only for Anksiyete is inconsistent. Either add 'bozukluğu' to Depresyon ('Depresif bozukluk') for parity or drop it from Anksiyete.
minor_issues.fix: Use 'Depresif bozukluk' and 'Anksiyete bozukluğu' as a pair (matches DSM-5-TR Turkish translation), or 'Depresyon' and 'Anksiyete' bare. Prefer the disorder forms for FHIR Condition.code.text.

minor_issues.issue: Adana weight (2.3) equals Konya (2.3), but TÜİK 2023 ADNKS puts Konya population (~2.32M) above Adana (~2.27M) — basically tied, OK — but Antalya 2.6 above Konya 2.3 is fine. Gaziantep 2.1 is roughly correct. Şanlıurfa 2.2 is reasonable. The bigger issue: a 'large-hospital EHR cohort' from Acibadem (Istanbul-based private group) would NOT have nationally-population-weighted province distribution — it would be heavily İstanbul/Ankara/İzmir-skewed because that is where Acibadem hospitals are. Population-weighted is the wrong prior.
minor_issues.fix: Document explicitly whether weights are TÜİK national population (the comment says so) or Acibadem-cohort empirical province distribution. If you want the synthetic patients to look like Acibadem patients, replace with the empirical province histogram from the source cohort. If you want them to look like Turkey, keep TÜİK weights — and say so.

minor_issues.quote: An in-app Collaborate panel surfaces live `help-wanted-clinician/dev/data` GitHub issues via the public GitHub API with a 15-minute localStorage cache.
minor_issues.issue: This is engineering trivia in a clinical-utility paragraph — feels like advertising rather than methods. Also unrelated to FHIR / clinical correctness.
minor_issues.fix: Move to a Software Engineering / Supplementary section. Or trim.

minor_issues.quote: Curation flags (29 columns: `pristine_*`, `berturk_*`, `tier_*`, `rule_clean`, `keyword_clean`, `nlp_filter_pass`, `rf_*`) are training-only metadata stripped from the default CSV before release (v0.5.6).
minor_issues.issue: berturk_* suggests a BERT-based Turkish NLP cleaner was applied to free-text notes; this should be cited (which Turkish BERT — BERTurk, mDeBERTa, etc.) and briefly described, because it materially affects what makes a record 'pristine'.
minor_issues.fix: Add one sentence: 'Free-text notes were screened by BERTurk-base (Schweter 2020) fine-tuned for clinical relevance; details in S6.' Or whichever model is actually used.

minor_issues.quote: Privacy is audited under the Stadler 2022 nearest-neighbor membership-inference attack (MIA).
minor_issues.issue: An MIA AUC of exactly 0.60 reported as 'gate held at ≤ 0.60' is suspiciously at the threshold. Reporting the 95% CI or the run-to-run variance would strengthen the claim — a single-point 0.60 with the gate at 0.60 invites scepticism.
minor_issues.fix: Report mean ± 95% CI across the nightly CI runs, e.g., 'mean MIA AUC 0.58 (95% CI 0.55–0.61) across 30 nightly runs, gate threshold 0.60'. Also state the holdout sample size and the number of shadow models.

minor_issues.quote: if pulse pressure $|SBP - DBP| < 20$ mmHg
minor_issues.issue: Note: pulse pressure is SBP − DBP, not |SBP − DBP| — DBP > SBP is itself unphysiologic and should be a separate rejection rule. Also, healthy young adults can have PP as low as 30; PP < 20 is reasonable as a hard floor but should cite Franklin et al. on pulse-pressure physiologic minima.
minor_issues.fix: Change to 'reject if SBP < DBP + 20'. Cite a pulse-pressure reference (e.g., Franklin SS, Circulation 1999).

minor_issues.quote: eGFR 6% + 1%/yr secular decline
minor_issues.issue: The 1%/yr eGFR decline is the population mean for healthy adults >40; younger adults decline closer to 0.4%/yr (Lindeman 1985; KDIGO 2024). For a 25-year-old in the cohort, 1%/yr is too steep.
minor_issues.fix: Use age-stratified decline: 0.4%/yr <40, 0.8%/yr 40–60, 1.0%/yr >60. Cite KDIGO 2024.

minor_issues.section: Methods – FHIR R4 export / Hyperlipidaemia module reference [21] Friedewald
minor_issues.quote: Friedewald residual $|TC - (HDL + LDL + TG/5)| > 40$ mg/dL
minor_issues.issue: Friedewald is unreliable when TG > 400 mg/dL — the constraint should be conditioned on TG ≤ 400, otherwise high-TG records will be falsely rejected. Most modern Turkish labs now use direct LDL or Martin-Hopkins above TG 200.
minor_issues.fix: Apply the Friedewald constraint only when TG ≤ 400 mg/dL, or switch to Martin-Hopkins estimation (Martin SS, JAMA 2013). Document in Methods.

minor_issues.quote: 17. Author(s). Differentially private synthesis of electronic health records via Gaussian-copula models. Front Digit Health. 2025.
minor_issues.issue: Reference [17] is an unfilled author placeholder ('Author(s)') — clearly a TODO that escaped review.
minor_issues.fix: Either fill in the actual citation or remove the reference and the corresponding citation pointer in §Discussion ('the DP-Gaussian-copula line [17]').

minor_issues.quote: Every Patient carries an `HTEST` tag plus a syntha-copula source tag (unambiguous "not a real human" marker).
minor_issues.issue: Excellent practice — but the HL7 v3 ActReason 'HTEST' is meta.security, not meta.tag. Confirm the actual placement to be HL7-compliant.
minor_issues.fix: State explicitly: 'meta.security carries v3-ActReason HTEST'. If currently placed in meta.tag, move it; FHIR conformance checkers will flag it.

reviews.summary: The manuscript describes a thoughtful hybrid Gaussian-copula synthetic EHR generator with genuine novelty in the Turkish locale + FHIR R4 + polyserial/tetrachoric estimator combination. However, the methodological exposition contains several errors and omissions that warrant major revision before publication. The Olsson polyserial formula is mis-stated (it is a two-step ML estimator, not a closed-form scaling of r_pb); the threshold form for binary variates is incomplete; the Frobenius difference 2.94 is reported without normalization or a baseline; the MIA AUC of 0.60 is reported as "the gate held" when AUC = the gate value is by definition borderline (not a margin); the privacy claim is framed responsibly in the Limitations but the Abstract/Results phrasing "gate held at MIA AUC ≤ 0.60" risks being read as a privacy guarantee; the nearest-PSD projection by "eigenvalue clipping" is glossed (no correlation re-normalization step described); oversample-and-reject convergence/acceptance rates are not reported; AR(1) parameters (the autocorrelation coefficient itself, separate from CVs) are not specified; seeded RNG and train/holdout splitting protocol are not described; and the paper compares qualitatively to Synthea/CTGAN/medGAN without any apples-to-apples benchmark (e.g., on SynthEHRella, which is cited as ref [18] but never used). Conditional missingness identifiability is also under-specified — the elementwise minimum rule is asserted without showing that the per-comorbidity conditional missing rate is estimable from observation alone. These are fixable with text-level revisions and one additional experiment/table.

critical_issues.section: Materials and Methods → Mixed-type correlation estimation
critical_issues.quote: For continuous–binary pairs we use the Olsson two-step polyserial estimator [11]: $\hat\rho = r_{pb} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{p(1-p)}}{\varphi(\Phi^{-1}(1-p))},$ where $r_{pb}$ is the point-biserial correlation.
critical_issues.issue: This is not the Olsson (1982) polyserial estimator. The formula shown is the classical biserial-from-point-biserial adjustment (Pearson 1909 / Lord & Novick), which assumes the dichotomous variable is a thresholded normal and the continuous variable is normal. Olsson, Drasgow & Dorans (1982) describe a two-step estimator in which (i) thresholds are estimated from the marginal of the ordinal/binary variable, and (ii) ρ is obtained by maximizing the conditional likelihood (or, in the original ad-hoc form, by a moment estimator that explicitly involves Σ φ(τ_k) under the ordinal categories). For a binary outcome the Olsson two-step and the biserial happen to coincide numerically when the continuous variable is exactly normal, but the manuscript's prose claims a 'two-step polyserial' is being applied — readers expecting Olsson will not find it. This conflation also undermines the claim that ECDF-based empirical marginals (i.e., non-normal continuous distributions) are being handled correctly, because the displayed formula assumes the continuous side is normal.
critical_issues.fix: Either (a) replace the formula with the actual Olsson two-step likelihood: estimate τ = Φ⁻¹(1−p) from the binary marginal, then maximize L(ρ) = Σ log[Φ((τ − ρ z_i)/√(1−ρ²))^{1−x_i} · (1 − Φ(…))^{x_i}] over ρ where z_i is the standardized rank-based score of the continuous variable; cite Olsson 1982 eqs. (4)–(6); or (b) acknowledge that, for binary outcomes, the implementation reduces to the biserial form and cite Lord & Novick 1968 plus Olsson 1982 §3. Clarify whether the continuous variable is standardized using its empirical CDF mapped through Φ⁻¹ before applying the formula (which would be the correct way to combine with the rest of the copula machinery).

critical_issues.quote: The Stadler 2022 nearest-synthetic-neighbor MIA, run nightly in CI against a 20% holdout, reported an AUC of 0.60 at the v0.5.8 release; the gate (AUC ≤ 0.60) held
critical_issues.issue: AUC = 0.60 with a gate of ≤ 0.60 is the boundary, not a margin. The Abstract phrasing 'the continuous-integration privacy gate held at MIA AUC ≤ 0.60' reads as a privacy guarantee, but (i) a single point estimate at the boundary has no reported confidence interval, (ii) the gate value 0.60 is arbitrary and not motivated against any threat-model literature, and (iii) AUC 0.60 is meaningfully above random (0.50) and corresponds to non-trivial leakage. The paper correctly states elsewhere that syntha is not yet differentially private, but the Abstract and Results frame the gate as if 'held' implies safety.
critical_issues.fix: Report (a) the bootstrap 95% CI for the AUC over shadow-cohort splits, (b) the rationale and citation for the 0.60 threshold (Stadler 2022 does not endorse it as a safety threshold), (c) reword the Abstract from 'the gate held at MIA AUC ≤ 0.60' to e.g. 'MIA AUC was 0.60 (95% CI …), at the CI gate; this is empirical, not a formal guarantee.' Mirror this rewording in §Results→Privacy.

critical_issues.section: Materials and Methods → Conditional, panel-aware missingness
critical_issues.quote: Stage 1: per-column $P(\text{missing} \mid \text{comorbidity-flag})$ rates are estimated and combined with marginal rates by elementwise minimum where the flag fires, encoding the empirical observation that sicker patients have *more* data.
critical_issues.issue: Identifiability is not established. P(missing | flag) is estimable from observed data, but the 'elementwise minimum' combination rule is ad hoc — it is not derived from any probability model, and there is no argument that the resulting bivariate missingness pattern matches the source. Crucially, the model is MAR-on-the-flag, but the flag itself can be missing or noisy; the manuscript does not say what happens when the comorbidity-flag observation is itself missing in the synthetic record. Also, the 0.85 panel co-missingness probability is stated as a parameter, not as something fit from data ('matching the source-cohort observation that all four lipid columns co-miss in >95% of episodes' — but the parameter is 0.85, not 0.95+; this discrepancy is unexplained).
critical_issues.fix: (a) State the missingness model formally: e.g. M_j ~ Bernoulli(min(p_j, p_{j|flag}·1[flag=1] + p_j·1[flag=0])), with panel indicator B ~ Bernoulli(0.85) selecting the all-co-miss branch; (b) justify the elementwise-minimum (or replace with a logistic regression on flags fit from observed data, which is identifiable under MAR); (c) reconcile 0.85 vs >95%, or report the source-cohort empirical co-miss rate that motivates 0.85; (d) state explicitly whether the flags themselves can be missing in the synthetic output.

critical_issues.quote: mean Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance was 0.058 (max 0.124); maximum binary-prevalence error 0.055; Spearman correlation Frobenius difference 2.94
critical_issues.issue: Three problems: (1) No baseline. KS=0.124 is 'good' relative to what? A naive marginal sampler? A Synthea bundle scored the same way? Two independent draws from the source (the irreducible sampling-noise floor)? Without a control, the reader cannot judge fidelity. (2) Frobenius difference 2.94 is unnormalized — for a d×d correlation matrix, ‖R_src − R_syn‖_F has scale Θ(d), so the number is uninterpretable without d and a baseline. (3) Asymptotic KS critical value at α=0.05 for n_1=n_2≈10⁵ is ≈0.006; KS=0.124 is therefore highly significant in the statistical-test sense — the manuscript needs to clarify it is using KS as a descriptive distance, not a hypothesis test, and that p-values are not meaningful at this n.
critical_issues.fix: Add a baseline column to Table 2: (i) source-vs-source resample KS (the irreducible floor), (ii) marginal-only synthetic (no copula) KS, (iii) Synthea or CTGAN trained on a comparable cohort if feasible. Report ‖R_src − R_syn‖_F / ‖R_src‖_F as a relative number, and give d. Explicitly note KS is a descriptive distance here and that p-values are uninformative at n>10^5.

major_issues.section: Materials and Methods → Gaussian copula formulation
major_issues.quote: a Bernoulli latent-threshold form $X = 1 \iff U \ge 1-p$ (fixed in v0.3.2) for binary variables
major_issues.issue: The threshold form is correct but the exposition skips the latent-Gaussian step that makes this a copula rather than just a marginal sampler. The reader should see: Z ~ N(0, R); U = Φ(Z); X = 1 iff U ≥ 1 − p, equivalently X = 1 iff Z ≥ Φ⁻¹(1 − p). This matters because the polyserial/tetrachoric estimators in the next subsection assume exactly this thresholded-Gaussian generative model — the equivalence is the whole point of why those estimators are the right ones.
major_issues.fix: Rewrite as: 'Binary variables are obtained by thresholding the corresponding latent Gaussian: X_j = 1 iff Z_j ≥ τ_j with τ_j = Φ⁻¹(1−p_j). Equivalently, with U_j = Φ(Z_j), X_j = 1 iff U_j ≥ 1−p_j. This is precisely the generative model assumed by the Olsson and tetrachoric estimators in §Mixed-type correlation estimation, which makes their use internally consistent.'

major_issues.section: Materials and Methods → Mixed-type correlation estimation
major_issues.quote: The estimated $\hat R$ is projected to the nearest positive-semidefinite matrix by eigenvalue clipping.
major_issues.issue: Eigenvalue clipping produces a PSD matrix but does not preserve unit diagonal — i.e. the result is in general not a valid correlation matrix. Standard practice (Higham 2002) is either to (i) clip eigenvalues, restore unit diagonal by D^{-1/2} Ã D^{-1/2}, iterate; or (ii) use Higham's alternating-projection algorithm onto the intersection of PSD and unit-diagonal sets. The manuscript should say which.
major_issues.fix: Specify the projection: e.g. 'We clip negative eigenvalues to ε=10⁻⁸, reconstruct, and rescale to unit diagonal via D⁻¹ᐟ² Ã D⁻¹ᐟ²; we verified the result remains PSD by a second eigendecomposition.' If Higham's algorithm is used, cite Higham 2002 (Linear Algebra Appl).

major_issues.section: Materials and Methods → Mixed-type correlation estimation
major_issues.quote: For continuous–continuous pairs we estimate Spearman $\rho_s$ and apply Kruskal's transform $\rho = 2\sin(\pi\rho_s/6)$ [16].
major_issues.issue: The relation ρ = 2 sin(π ρ_s / 6) is Pearson-of-bivariate-normal from Spearman, and is exact only under bivariate normality. With ECDF-based empirical marginals (so each variable is pushed through its own ECDF before the latent step), the variables on the copula scale are uniform, and the relation is then asymptotically correct as a Gaussian-copula estimator — but this should be stated, with a citation to Kendall & Stuart or Kruskal 1958 in context.
major_issues.fix: Add one sentence: 'This relation is exact under a Gaussian copula, which is the model we are fitting; for non-Gaussian dependence, it serves as a moment-type estimator with bias O(1/n).'

major_issues.quote: Oversampling factor 1.5 with up to five retry rounds is applied at the pipeline level.
major_issues.issue: No acceptance-rate statistics are reported. Five rounds at oversample 1.5 = at most 1.5^5 ≈ 7.6× draws; if the filter rejects a non-trivial fraction this changes the marginal distributions of the surviving cohort and could explain part of the 0.124 KS. Selection bias from rejection sampling is unaddressed.
major_issues.fix: Report the empirical acceptance rate per constraint and overall, the round at which generation typically completes, and whether the post-filter marginals were re-checked against the source. If acceptance is very high (>99%) say so; if not, discuss the marginal-distortion implications.

major_issues.section: Materials and Methods → Longitudinal expansion and AR(1) lab drift
major_issues.quote: Per-lab time series are reconstructed by an AR(1) walk backward from the cross-sectional `_latest` value, using column-specific Westgard analytical CVs (eGFR 6% + 1%/yr secular decline, HbA1c $\sigma$ ≈ 0.3%, Hb 2%, ALT/AST 15%, TG 15%).
major_issues.issue: The AR(1) parameter itself — the autoregression coefficient φ — is never given. CVs describe the marginal noise σ but the temporal persistence (φ in X_t = φ X_{t−1} + ε_t) is the load-bearing parameter for any longitudinal validation. Also, walking 'backward from the latest value' is unusual: AR(1) is time-reversible only when stationary; if the secular decline of 1%/yr is being applied, the process is non-stationary and backward simulation must explicitly model the mean trajectory. Source for the CVs (Westgard 1981 [22]) is for QC of analytical replicates, not for between-encounter biological variation — those are different quantities (CV_a vs CV_g).
major_issues.fix: Report φ per analyte (or state φ = 1, i.e. random walk, if that is what is implemented). Distinguish analytical CV (instrument noise) from intra-individual biological CV (Fraser & Harris) — only the latter is appropriate for between-encounter drift. Specify the backward-simulation step including how the secular trend is incorporated.

major_issues.quote: Pure data-driven deep generators (medGAN [3], CorGAN [4], CTGAN [5], DPGAN [7], PATE-GAN [8], EHR-Safe [9]) recover joint distributions but require large training sets, mode-collapse on rare comorbidities, and resist formal privacy proofs at low $\varepsilon$
major_issues.issue: No head-to-head comparison is reported, yet the Discussion makes specific qualitative claims about how syntha compares (interpretability, runtime, mode collapse). The paper cites SynthEHRella (ref [18]) but never uses it, even though it is precisely the benchmark suite for this comparison. The Comparison-fairness reviewer concern: this is not an apples-to-apples comparison and the Discussion should not be framed as if it were.
major_issues.fix: Either (a) run syntha through the SynthEHRella benchmark and report the comparison on at least KS, pairwise correlation, and MIA AUC alongside CTGAN/medGAN/Synthea; or (b) soften the Discussion to 'syntha is designed to occupy a different point in the design space — interpretable parameters and small training cohorts — rather than to outperform deep generators on large US datasets; a head-to-head benchmark on SynthEHRella is deferred to future work.'

major_issues.section: Materials and Methods → Privacy audit / Results → Privacy
major_issues.quote: (i) a nearest-synthetic-neighbor membership-inference attack (Stadler 2022 [10]) reporting ROC-AUC against a held-out shadow cohort
major_issues.issue: Shadow-cohort construction is unspecified. Stadler 2022's NN-MIA requires a shadow training set, a shadow holdout, and a target model; reporting just 'a 20% holdout' (mentioned in Results) does not say how the shadow cohort is sampled, how many trials are averaged, or what distance metric the NN attack uses (Euclidean on standardized features? Gower for mixed types?). Reproducibility of the privacy number is therefore unclear.
major_issues.fix: In §Privacy audit add: shadow-cohort sampling protocol, distance metric used by the NN attacker, number of shadow draws averaged, and reference the supplementary section S2 for the full protocol. Pin the random seed used for the CI run that produced the headline AUC=0.60.

major_issues.quote: (no quote — observation about an absence)
major_issues.issue: Seeded RNG and train/holdout splitting protocol are nowhere reported in the main text. Reproducibility of all reported numbers (KS, Frobenius, MIA AUC) requires a seed and a split spec. The paper says 'every figure, table, and number in this manuscript is regenerated by scripts/make_plots.py and pytest -q', but the seed used by those scripts is not in the manuscript.
major_issues.fix: Add a 'Reproducibility' subsection (or one line in each numbers-producing subsection) stating: NumPy/PyTorch RNG seed used, train/holdout split fractions and stratification variable, and that the seed is fixed in scripts/make_plots.py. Report whether reported numbers are single-seed point estimates or means ± SD over k seeds (and if single-seed, justify).

major_issues.section: Materials and Methods → Mixed-type correlation estimation
major_issues.quote: Empirically this fixes a ~50% magnitude attenuation (≈65% on binary–binary) introduced by passing raw Spearman through Kruskal on tied binary columns
major_issues.issue: The '~50%' and '≈65%' attenuation numbers are stated without a supporting figure, table, or supplementary derivation. These are quantitative empirical claims about a methodological choice and need a citation to a panel in the Results, the Supplement, or a simulation.
major_issues.fix: Either point to Figure 2 / a supplementary table that demonstrates the attenuation numerically (with a known-truth simulation, ideally), or add such a panel to the Supplement and cite it here ('see Supplementary Figure S-X for a simulation with known R').

minor_issues.quote: Mean Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance was 0.058 (max 0.124)
minor_issues.issue: Two decimals in Abstract, four in Results body ('0.0576', 'max 0.1236') — minor inconsistency.
minor_issues.fix: Pick three significant figures consistently across Abstract, Results, and Table 2.

minor_issues.section: Materials and Methods → FHIR R4 export
minor_issues.quote: RiskAssessment (Charlson Comorbidity Index, LOINC 75618-7; calibrated 10-year mortality $P = 1 - 0.983^{0.9\cdot\text{CCI}}$)
minor_issues.issue: Charlson's original 10-year mortality formula uses the form 0.983^(e^{0.9·CCI}) — note the exponential of 0.9·CCI, not the linear term as written. Verify against Charlson 1987 (ref [20]).
minor_issues.fix: Rewrite as P = 1 − 0.983^{exp(0.9·CCI)} per Charlson et al. 1987, or state explicitly that a linearized approximation is used and justify it.

minor_issues.section: Materials and Methods → Conditional, panel-aware missingness
minor_issues.quote: matching the source-cohort observation that all four lipid columns co-miss in >95% of episodes
minor_issues.issue: Four lipid columns, but elsewhere the panel grouping is by LOINC 57698-3 (lipid panel) which historically contains five components (TC, HDL, LDL, TG, non-HDL or Chol/HDL ratio). State which four are meant.
minor_issues.fix: Specify: 'the four lipid analytes (TC, HDL, LDL, TG)'.

minor_issues.quote: 17. Author(s). Differentially private synthesis of electronic health records via Gaussian-copula models. Front Digit Health. 2025.
minor_issues.issue: Reference 17 is a placeholder ('Author(s).'). This must be a real citation before publication.
minor_issues.fix: Replace with the actual author list, volume, and pages, or remove the citation and the corresponding claim in Limitations (ii).

minor_issues.quote: (iv) The polyserial/tetrachoric implementation, although validated by simulation, has not yet been benchmarked head-to-head against R's `polycor`
minor_issues.issue: Given that the polyserial/tetrachoric choice is one of the paper's two main methodological contributions, validating against polycor (Fox) on a small simulation is a low-effort, high-value addition and should be done before publication rather than deferred.
minor_issues.fix: Run the polycor comparison on a 1000-sample simulation with known R and report mean absolute error on the off-diagonal in the Supplement; move this out of Limitations.

minor_issues.section: Materials and Methods → Source cohort and curation
minor_issues.quote: Two flags consumed by the FHIR exporter (`rf_kanser`, `rf_kronik_hastalik`) are read before stripping.
minor_issues.issue: These flag names are introduced without a definition in the main text — only readers familiar with the upstream pipeline will know what 'rf_' denotes. Briefly define.
minor_issues.fix: Add one parenthetical: '(`rf_kanser` = random-forest-derived cancer indicator; `rf_kronik_hastalik` = chronic-disease indicator)'.

minor_issues.quote: consistent with the analytic expectation that a 200-quantile + correlation-matrix summary leaks little record-level information
minor_issues.issue: 'Analytic expectation' is asserted, not derived. The bound on information leakage from quantile + correlation summaries is not a trivial result — a citation or one-line argument is needed.
minor_issues.fix: Either cite a result bounding information leakage from histogram-style summaries (e.g., the smoothed-empirical-distribution literature), or rephrase to 'consistent with the small number of sufficient statistics released' without claiming this is an analytic bound.

minor_issues.section: Materials and Methods → Mixed-type correlation estimation
minor_issues.quote: evaluating the bivariate-normal CDF with Drezner's 8-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature [13]
minor_issues.issue: Drezner 1978 [13] uses a specific Gauss–Hermite-like 5-point and 8-point scheme depending on the sign of the correlation; specifying '8-point' alone is incomplete (and the 8-point variant in Drezner 1978 is for |ρ| > 0.7). Drezner & Wesolowsky 1990 is the more commonly cited extension. Confirm which is implemented.
minor_issues.fix: Check the implementation in src/syntha/... and state precisely whether it is Drezner 1978 (with the |ρ|-dependent branch) or Drezner & Wesolowsky 1990. Cite accordingly.

specific_edits.from: the joint distribution of a $d$-dimensional clinical vector is decomposed into $d$ univariate marginals and a copula function. syntha uses a Gaussian copula: latent multivariate-normal variates $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R)$ are pushed through column-specific marginals — empirical CDFs for continuous variables and a Bernoulli latent-threshold form $X = 1 \iff U \ge 1-p$ (fixed in v0.3.2) for binary variables.
specific_edits.to: the joint distribution of a $d$-dimensional clinical vector is decomposed into $d$ univariate marginals and a copula. syntha uses a Gaussian copula with correlation matrix $R$: draw $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R)$, set $U_j = \Phi(Z_j)$ on the uniform scale, and map back to the data scale via column-specific marginals — empirical CDFs $\hat F_j^{-1}(U_j)$ for continuous variables, and the threshold rule $X_j = 1 \iff Z_j \ge \Phi^{-1}(1-p_j)$ (equivalently $U_j \ge 1-p_j$) for binary variables. This thresholded-Gaussian generative model is exactly the model under which the polyserial and tetrachoric estimators of the next subsection are consistent.
specific_edits.rationale: Makes the latent-Gaussian step explicit and ties the copula construction to the estimator choice.

specific_edits.from: $$\hat\rho = r_{pb} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{p(1-p)}}{\varphi(\Phi^{-1}(1-p))},$$ where $r_{pb}$ is the point-biserial correlation.
specific_edits.to: we estimate the threshold $\hat\tau = \Phi^{-1}(1-\hat p)$ from the binary marginal and then estimate $\rho$ by maximizing the conditional log-likelihood $\sum_i [x_i \log(1-\Phi(\frac{\hat\tau - \rho z_i}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}})) + (1-x_i)\log \Phi(\frac{\hat\tau - \rho z_i}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}})]$, where $z_i = \Phi^{-1}(\hat F(y_i))$ is the continuous variable mapped to the latent-Gaussian scale via its empirical CDF (Olsson 1982, eqs. 4–6). For the special case of a Gaussian continuous variable this reduces to the closed-form biserial $\hat\rho = r_{pb}\sqrt{p(1-p)}/\varphi(\Phi^{-1}(1-p))$.
specific_edits.rationale: Aligns the stated formula with the cited Olsson 1982 method and the ECDF marginals used elsewhere in the pipeline.

specific_edits.from: The estimated $\hat R$ is projected to the nearest positive-semidefinite matrix by eigenvalue clipping.
specific_edits.to: The estimated $\hat R$ is projected to the nearest valid correlation matrix by clipping negative eigenvalues to $\varepsilon=10^{-8}$, reconstructing, and rescaling to unit diagonal via $D^{-1/2}\tilde R D^{-1/2}$; we verified PSD-ness of the result by a second eigendecomposition (Higham 2002).
specific_edits.rationale: Makes the PSD-projection step reproducible and ensures the output is a correlation matrix, not just a PSD matrix.

specific_edits.from: The continuous-integration privacy gate held at MIA AUC ≤ 0.60.
specific_edits.to: The continuous-integration privacy gate (MIA AUC ≤ 0.60) was met, with point estimate 0.60 (95% bootstrap CI to be reported); this is an empirical check, not a formal differential-privacy guarantee.
specific_edits.rationale: Removes the implicit safety guarantee, addressing the reviewer concern that 0.60 at the gate boundary is not a margin.

specific_edits.from: Oversampling factor 1.5 with up to five retry rounds is applied at the pipeline level.
specific_edits.to: Oversampling factor 1.5 with up to five retry rounds is applied at the pipeline level; empirical first-round acceptance under the three physiologic constraints was X% on the v0.5.8 release (Supplementary Table S-Y), and marginal distributions of accepted vs. drawn rows differed by KS ≤ Z, ruling out material selection bias.
specific_edits.rationale: Quantifies the acceptance rate and explicitly addresses post-rejection marginal distortion.

specific_edits.from: Per-lab time series are reconstructed by an AR(1) walk backward from the cross-sectional `_latest` value, using column-specific Westgard analytical CVs
specific_edits.to: Per-lab time series are reconstructed by an AR(1) process $X_t = \mu_t + \phi(X_{t-1} - \mu_{t-1}) + \varepsilon_t$ with $\phi = $ [value], $\mu_t$ encoding any secular trend (e.g. eGFR 1%/yr decline), and $\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ where $\sigma$ is derived from published intra-individual biological CVs (Fraser 2001) rather than purely analytical CVs, since between-encounter variation is dominated by within-subject biological variability
specific_edits.rationale: Adds the missing autoregression coefficient and corrects the CV-type conflation; analytical CV (Westgard) and biological CV are different quantities.

reviews.summary: syntha is a credible and well-engineered Application Note describing a hybrid Gaussian-copula synthetic EHR generator with Turkish localization and FHIR R4 export. The technical contribution is plausible and the engineering disclosures (CI, signing, coverage) are strong. However, the manuscript has several issues that would trigger a major revision: (1) the ethics/IRB statement is hand-waved — no IRB number, no approving committee named, no description of the de-identification method beyond "anonymized retrospectively by the institutional data steward"; (2) reference 17 is a literal placeholder ("Author(s)") and references 18 and 19 lack volume/page/DOI; (3) figures are referenced by filename rather than reproduced or fully captioned with sample sizes, statistical tests, and axis labels; (4) the novelty claim ("first openly available FHIR-R4-coded generator calibrated to a Turkish hospital cohort") is plausible but not supported by a systematic search and partially undercut by ref 19 (Yıldız 2022); (5) the MIA "AUC of 0.60 at the gate" with gate "≤ 0.60" is precisely at the threshold and the report does not disclose CI or n-shadow — a competing reviewer will pounce; (6) the data-availability statement says a Zenodo DOI is "cross-referenced" but does not provide the DOI; (7) the word count appears slightly over the 2000-word Application Note limit. Recommend major revision.

critical_issues.issue: Reference 17 is an unfilled placeholder citation, which would trigger desk-reject by any copy editor.
critical_issues.quote: 17. Author(s). Differentially private synthesis of electronic health records via Gaussian-copula models. Front Digit Health. 2025.
critical_issues.fix: Replace with the actual author list, volume, issue, page range and DOI, or remove the citation and the supporting sentence in Limitations ('following the DP-Gaussian-copula line [17]').

critical_issues.issue: IRB status is hand-waved. The journal requires explicit disclosure of the approving ethics committee, approval number, date, and the de-identification mechanism. 'Anonymized retrospectively by the institutional data steward' is not a substitute and does not state whether the Acibadem University Ethics Committee reviewed the secondary use, nor what HIPAA/KVKK-equivalent standard was applied.
critical_issues.quote: Ethics: the source dataset was anonymized retrospectively by the institutional data steward; this work involved no patient interaction.
critical_issues.fix: Add a dedicated Ethics statement naming the approving committee (e.g., 'Acibadem University Medical Research Ethics Committee, approval number ATADEK-XXXX, dated YYYY-MM-DD'), describe whether the secondary use was reviewed or deemed exempt, name the de-identification standard applied (e.g., HIPAA Safe Harbor, KVKK Article X, or a Statistical Disclosure Control method with k-anonymity threshold), state who held the linkage key and whether it was destroyed, and confirm that no re-identification was attempted.

critical_issues.issue: The Zenodo DOI is promised but not provided, which violates JAMIA Open's data-availability requirements and prevents archival reproducibility.
critical_issues.quote: Archived release: deposited at Zenodo with a DOI cross-referenced from the GitHub release page
critical_issues.fix: Provide the literal Zenodo DOI (e.g., 10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXX) at the time of submission. A 'see GitHub release page' redirect is not acceptable for an immutable archival deposit.

major_issues.issue: The MIA result of AUC=0.60 sits exactly at the CI gate threshold of ≤0.60. Without a confidence interval, shadow-cohort size, or number of MIA replicates, a reviewer cannot tell whether the gate actually held in a statistically meaningful sense or whether the gate was tuned to the observed value.
major_issues.quote: the v0.5.8 release; the gate (AUC ≤ 0.60) held, consistent with the analytic expectation
major_issues.fix: Report MIA AUC as a point estimate plus 95% CI (e.g., bootstrap over the shadow cohort), state the shadow-cohort n and number of replicates, and justify the 0.60 threshold against published guidance (e.g., Stadler 2022 §5 or El Emam guidance). Ideally report AUC strictly less than the gate (e.g., 0.54 with 95% CI [0.51, 0.58]).

major_issues.issue: The 'first openly available FHIR-R4-coded generator calibrated to a Turkish hospital cohort' is made twice but is not supported by a systematic search description, and reference 19 (Yıldız 2022, 'Calibrating synthetic patient cohorts to Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) demographic marginals') directly suggests prior Turkish-locale work that is not discussed.
major_issues.quote: The Turkish-locale contribution is, to our knowledge, the first openly available fully FHIR-R4-coded generator calibrated to a Turkish hospital cohort
major_issues.fix: Add a sentence explicitly comparing to Yıldız 2022 [19] (was it open source? did it emit FHIR? was it calibrated to a hospital cohort or only to TÜİK marginals?) and describe the search strategy used to establish novelty (databases searched, date, query). Soften 'first' to a defensible claim if the search was not systematic.

major_issues.issue: Figures 1–3 are referenced only by filename. Captions do not state sample sizes per panel, axis labels, units, statistical test, or whether the synthetic sample is one realization or pooled across realizations. JAMIA Open requires self-contained figure captions.
major_issues.quote: Figure 1 (`docs/figures/distributions.png`) overlays empirical density estimates for the principal continuous analytes

However, three limitations recur: they require GPU training, their parameters are not interpretable to clinicians, and they remain vulnerable to membership-inference attacks even when wrapped in differential-privacy mechanisms [10].

specific_edits.from: A two-stage missingness model replaces the v0.4 independent column-Bernoulli "Swiss-cheese" missingness. Stage 1: per-column $P(\text{missing} \mid \text{comorbidity-flag})$ rates are estimated and combined with marginal rates by elementwise minimum where the flag fires, encoding the empirical observation that sicker patients have *more* data.
specific_edits.to: A two-stage missingness model supersedes the column-independent Bernoulli model used in v0.4. In stage 1, per-column P(missing | comorbidity-flag) rates are estimated and combined with the marginal missingness rate by elementwise minimum where the flag fires, reflecting the empirical observation that patients with more comorbidities are observed more densely (i.e., have fewer missing values).

reviews.summary: A well-structured Application Note that is publishable with minor revisions. The science argument flows cleanly and the Methods/Results pairing is mostly tight. Key editorial issues: (1) several reported numbers in the abstract (Frobenius 2.94, max KS 0.124, MIA AUC 0.60) lack interpretive context for the non-expert reader; (2) Reference 17 contains a literal 'Author(s)' placeholder and refs 18–26 are not cited inline — these are blocking errors; (3) several acronyms (AUC/AUROC, AIA, ACEi/ARB/SSRI/ICS/SABA/LAMA/LABA, TÜİK, CDF, BVN) are used without first-use expansion; (4) numeric precision is inconsistent between abstract and Results (0.058 vs 0.0576); (5) Figures 1–3 are described inline but lack standalone captions; (6) Table 2 needs unit/notation footnotes and should report the observed AIA AUCs, not just the threshold; (7) the Methods section drifts briefly into conversational tone ('Swiss-cheese', italicized 'more'); and (8) the 'first to our knowledge' claim is made three times — keep it once. Overall the paper reads professionally and the structure is sound, but a careful editorial sweep is required before acceptance.

Most reproducibility scaffolding is present: pyproject.toml pins Python >=3.10 and library minimums, a Docker tag (ghcr.io/ariomoniri/syntha:v0.5.8) is given, scripts/make_plots.py exists with N_SYNTHETIC=5000 and SEED=42, .github/workflows/privacy-audit.yml runs a deterministic seeded audit (rng default_rng(42), 80/20 split, GaussianCopulaGenerator(random_seed=0)), and signed installer artifacts have stable GitHub/PyPI/GHCR URLs. However, the manuscript itself does not surface several of these load-bearing details (e.g. SEED=42 for figures, the exact CI workflow path for the desktop build, the bundled-model JSON path scripts/make_plots.py actually reads, the audit's specific train/test split seed and shadow-cohort construction, and the exact MIA hyperparameters). The Zenodo DOI is described as "deposited" but not cited with an actual identifier. Several Results numbers (Charlson 0.9 scaling, AR(1) Westgard CVs) reference code constants that are not located by file/function in the manuscript. These are minor and can be fixed with targeted additions to the Reproducibility paragraph and a small expansion in the Data and Code Availability section.
